fields.title: Falls and Fractures in Older Adults: Causes and Prevention
fields.text:
From the National Institutes on Aging: More than one in four people age 65 years or older fall each year. The risk of falling — and fall-related problems — rises with age. However, many falls can be prevented. For example, exercising, managing your medications, having your vision checked, and making your home safer are all steps you can take to prevent a fall. 

Learn more about falls [here](https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/falls-and-falls-prevention/falls-and-fractures-older-adults-causes-and-prevention).

fields.title: A Good Night's Sleep
fields.text:
According to the National Institute on Aging, "being older doesn't mean you have to be tired all the time. You can do many things to help you get a good night's sleep:"

Follow a regular sleep schedule. 
Avoid napping in the late afternoon or evening, if you can. 
Develop a bedtime routine. 
Try not to watch television or use your computer, cell phone, or tablet in the bedroom. 
Keep your bedroom at a comfortable temperature.
Use low lighting in the evenings.
Exercise at regular times each day but not within 3 hours of your bedtime.
Avoid eating large meals close to bedtime.
Stay away from caffeine late in the day. 
Remember—alcohol won’t help you sleep. 

Read more about sleep [here](https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/sleep/good-nights-sleep).

fields.title: Advance Care Planning
fields.text:
According to the National Institute on Aging, "Advance care planning involves discussing and preparing for future decisions about your medical care if you become seriously ill or unable to communicate your wishes. Having meaningful conversations with your loved ones is the most important part of advance care planning. Many people also choose to put their preferences in writing by completing legal documents called advance directives."

How to get started: 
Reflect on your values and wishes.
Talk with your doctor about advance directives.
Choose someone you trust to make medical decisions for you.
Complete your advance directive forms.
Share your forms with your health care agent, doctors and loved ones. 
Keep the conversation going.

Read more about Advance Care Planning [here](https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/advance-care-planning/advance-care-planning-advance-directives-health-care)

fields.title: Where can you find reliable health information?
fields.text:
[Medline Plus](https://medlineplus.gov) is the most reliable source of health information in the US. It is run by the National Library of Medicine (NLM), the world's largest medical library, which is part of the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

It offers quality, accurate, and up-to-date health and wellness information. The site is free of advertising, and it is in both English and Spanish. Look up a health topic and learn [here](https://medlineplus.gov/healthtopics.html)

fields.title: Age-related Hearing Loss (Presbycusis)
fields.text:
Age-related hearing loss is a common problem as we get older. Nearly a third of people between 65 and 74 have trouble hearing, and that number increases to nearly half of people over 75. According to the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders, "to help safeguard your hearing as you age, avoid loud noises, reduce the amount of time you're exposed to loud sounds, and protect your ears with earplugs or protective earmuffs."
Learn more about age-related hearing loss [here](https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/age-related-hearing-loss).

fields.title: Dermatologists' Tips for Relieving Dry Skin
fields.text:
Dry skin is a very common problem, but there are ways to prevent or relieve it. Here are some tips from the American Academy of Dermatology: 

1. Use 5- to 10-minute baths and showers to hydrate your dry skin.
2. Apply moisturizer immediately after washing.
3. Use an ointment or cream rather than a lotion. 
4. Wear lip balm or apply petroleum jelly to your lips.
5. Use only gentle, fragrance-free skin care products. 
6. Wear gloves.
7. Choose non-irritating clothes and laundry detergent. 
8. Stay warm without cozying up to a fireplace or other heat source.
9. Add moisture to the air.


Check out this [infographic](https://assets.ctfassets.net/1ny4yoiyrqia/JxLNwZ6cuGJhOx4XttiU7/3282875415de5daa7169320d9333d981/Bathing_tips_for_dry_skin_relief_infographic.pdf). 

Read more about dry skin [here](https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-basics/dry/dermatologists-tips-relieve-dry-skin).

fields.title: Herbs and Supplements
fields.text:
They may not be called "drugs," but herbs and supplements can have positive and negative effects on your health and may interact with the prescription medications you are taking. They also can be very expensive. Are they effective? 

Here are [five tips](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/tips/tips-what-consumers-need-to-know-about-dietary-supplements) from the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health: 

1. Take charge of your health by being an informed consumer.
2. "Natural" does not necessarily mean "safe."
3. Interactions are possible.
4. Be aware of the potential for contamination.
5. Talk to your healthcare providers. 

MedlinePlus offers information about the effectiveness of many supplements, including dosing and drug interactions [here](https://medlineplus.gov/druginfo/herb_All.html).

fields.title: Walking for Older Adults
fields.text:
Walking is the most popular form of exercise among older adults, and it's a great choice.

What can walking do for you? Walking can:

    - strengthen muscles
    - help prevent weight gain
    - lower risks of heart disease, stroke, diabetes, and osteoporosis
    - improve balance
    - lower the likelihood of falling

If you have not exercised for a long time, you may want to start out slowly.  You can start with just 5 minutes and build up to the recommended 30 minutes a day. Your goal should be to get up to taking 100 steps a minute. Remember, the most important thing is just to get started. 

Learn more about walking [here](https://www.healthinaging.org/tools-and-tips/tip-sheet-walking-older-adult from the American Geriatrics Society's Health in Aging program

fields.title: Preventing Serious Falls
fields.text:
Falls are a leading cause of serious injuries in older adults that can lead to hospitalization, nursing home admission, and even death among older people. 

The chance of falling increases as we get older. Health problems such as arthritis, heart disease, muscle weakness, poor balance or vision, foot problems, Parkinson’s disease, dementia, and even certain medications can increase your chance of falling.  Dangerous things around the home – slippery throw rugs and poor lighting, for example – make falls more likely as well.  If you are an older adult or in charge of care for an older person, please follow the steps below and regularly get a “falls checkup” from your healthcare provider. 

- Tell your healthcare provider if you have had a fall.
- Review your medications.
- Make a falls prevention plan with your healthcare provider.
- Exercise to prevent falls.
- Make your home safe from falls.

Learn more from the American Geriatrics Society's Health in Aging program [here](https://www.healthinaging.org/tools-and-tips/tip-sheet-preventing-serious-falls).

fields.title: Finding Health Information on the Internet
fields.text:
We are living in the information age. The Internet is a useful tool that allows us to keep up with friends and family, follow the news, shop, share photos, and much more—all of which can benefit an older adult. What’s more, the Internet can be a convenient place to get the answers to many of your health questions, right from the comfort of your living room. But with so many health websites available, how can you find reliable, safe advice?

Fortunately, you can take smart, easy steps to make sure that the information you read on the Internet is accurate, safe, and based on expert advice. Here’s how:

- Know the source (check the web address).
- Look for the site's contact information.
- Look for recognized experts as writers and reviewers.
- Check the review date.
- Be careful.

Find out more information from the American Geriatrics Society's Health in Aging Program [here](https://www.healthinaging.org/tools-and-tips/tip-sheet-safely-surfing-internet).

Read the JAMA Internal Medicine Patient Page [here](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/2817486).

fields.title: Tips To Keep Your Bladder Healthy
fields.text:
People rarely talk about bladder health, but everyone is affected by it. The bladder is a hollow organ, much like a balloon, that stores urine. Urine contains waste and extra fluid left over after the body takes what it needs from what we eat and drink. Each day, adults pass about a quart and a half of urine through the bladder and out of the body.

As people get older, their bladder changes. Once very elastic, the bladder tissue may lose flexibility and become less stretchy. A less flexible bladder cannot hold as much urine as before and might make you go to the bathroom more often. The bladder wall and pelvic floor muscles may weaken, making it harder to empty the bladder fully and causing urine to leak.

Here are some steps to keep your bladder healthy: 

- Drink enough fluids, especially water. 
- Do pelvic floor exercises.
- Wear cotton underwear and loose-fitting clothing.
- Use the bathroom when needed, and take the time to empty your bladder fully.
- Watch what you eat, and avoid foods that irritate your bladder. 

You can learn more from the American Geriatrics Society's Health in Aging Program [here](https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/bladder-health-and-incontinence/15-tips-keep-your-bladder-healthy)

fields.title: Tips for People Worried About Memory Loss
fields.text:
We are at greater risk for memory loss and dementia as we age. Here are some healthy behaviors that can reduce your risk: 

- Take part in regular physical activity.
- Engage in challenging mental activities.
- Manage your medical conditions like hypertension, diabetes, and high cholesterol.
- Eat a healthy diet. 
- Limit alcohol and tobacco use. 
- Spend time with family and friends. 

Learn more from the JAMA Internal Medicine Patient Page [here](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/2815815).

fields.title: HIV and Bones
fields.text:
As you age, your bones tend to get weaker. If you have the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), this may be especially true. The virus, which causes AIDS, may make your bones more likely to break. Furthermore, some anti-HIV medications may raise your chances for bone loss.

Bone mineral density tests (DEXA scans) are usually recommended for women after menopause and men after 50 in the HIV+ population. 

Protect your bones by: 
- Not smoking.
- Limiting alcohol consumption - it's best not to drink alcohol at all.
- Exercising.
- Eating foods that are high in calcium and vitamin D. 

To learn more, read this WebMD article [here](https://www.webmd.com/hiv-aids/hiv-bone-health-link).

fields.title: Participating in research studies
fields.text:
You are participating in one now and helping improve the quality of healthcare. 
According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), the benefits of participating in clinical trials include: 

 - You may have the chance to help scientists better understand your disease or condition and to advance treatments and ways to prevent it in the future.
 - You may feel like you’re playing a more active role in your health.
 - You may learn more about your disease or condition.
 - You may be able to get information about support groups and resources.
 
The NIA has more information about clinical trials [here](https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/clinical-trials-and-studies/clinical-research-benefits-risks-and-safety).

fields.title: COPPEHR is Starting Soon!
fields.text:
The IRB has approved our study. 
Stay tuned!
Look out for fliers with information. If you participated in the focus groups, expect a call inviting you to join this second phase. 
Everyone receives a free Chromebook.

fields.title: Men's Health
fields.series_title: Weill Cornell Medicine Patient Care Events
fields.description:
The American Cancer Society reports that prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death in American men, behind lung cancer. Testicular cancer also affects men, but it is rare. Both are highly treatable.

Join this Men's Health session to understand the signs, symptoms, and treatment methods for both during the Weill Cornell Medicine Wellness Series with the Harry Belafonte 115th Street Library.

Presenter: 
Bashir Al Hussein Al Awamlh, MD, MPH, is an Assistant Professor of Urology at Weill Cornell Medicine

This is a virtual event and registration is required: on.nypl.org/3XdJmB9

fields.title: National HIV and Aging Awareness Day
fields.description: National HIV/AIDS and Aging Awareness Day (NHAAD) is observed each year on September 18 to focus on the increasing number of people who, because of major advancements in HIV treatment, are living long, full lives with HIV. The awareness day also calls attention to the unique health and social needs, as well as the challenges of HIV prevention, testing, treatment, and care among people who are aging.
fields.art_caption: Logo for HIV and Awareness Day

fields.title: New HIV meds - Are they right for me?
fields.description:
Should I switch to one of the newer HIV medications or stay with what’s working for me? 

At this Ask the Expert session, hear about new available medications and others under development. Ask the expert about the advantages, disadvantages, and possible side effects. Gain insights on how these treatments compare to existing options and their potential impact on current treatment strategies.

fields.title: How to be happy and how to build resilience
fields.description:
How can I use mindfulness to feel happier and stronger? What are some simple ways to start?

Join our mental health experts as we explore issues surrounding mindfulness, resilience, and happiness.  This Ask the Expert session will provide training in mindfulness techniques, describe habits to help cultivate happiness in our lives, and review strategies to build resilience.  Bring your questions about finding more satisfaction in your day-to-day life and overcoming the challenges, anxiety, and fear that come along the way.

fields.title: Cancer & cancer screening in older adults living with HIV
fields.description:
When can I stop getting colonoscopies? Should I have my prostate checked? Do I need to be screened for lung cancer? 

Join our medical experts in this Ask the Expert session to hear about key guidelines for cancer screening in older adults with HIV.  Learn more about how cancer screening guidelines are developed, what cancers you should be screened for, at what ages we can stop screening, and instances where screening might not be appropriate. Ask experts about which tests are currently recommended.

fields.title: Vaccinations and Preventative Care in HIV
fields.description:
Should I continue to get the COVID booster? Do I need to take an aspirin a day? 

Join our primary care experts to learn about how healthcare providers strive to help you prevent illness.  During this Ask the Expert session, we will answer questions about current vaccination recommendations, screening tests recommended to prevent the development of conditions like heart disease and diabetes, and share daily practices you can follow to maintain your health.

fields.title: Sexual health in HIV and STIs screening
fields.description:
In the immortal words of Salt-N-Pepa, “Lets Talk about Sex.”  

This Ask the Expert session will be led by our infectious disease experts and primary care doctors, who will share the most up-to-date information about practicing safe sex while positively promoting a satisfying sex life for older adults.  They will be there to answer questions about STI prevention, testing, treatment, and the impact of other conditions on sexual health as we age.

fields.title: Social work session
fields.description:
Do I have the right medicare insurance plan? Can I get someone to help around my home? Are there local resources that I can use to get additional food and housing support? 

Our experienced social workers are here to guide you. Please join them during this month's Ask the Expert session to gain insight into the resources available to support you as you age in your community.

fields.title: Depression and Anxiety
fields.description:
Have you been feeling down or depressed recently? Do you find yourself worrying about many different things? 

During this month's Ask the Expert session, you will hear our mental health providers share an overview of what depression and anxiety can look like, how we diagnose it, how we treat it with both behavioral and pharmacologic therapy, and special consideration in the HIV-positive population.  They will take your questions about mental health, finding treatment, and supporting loved ones experiencing mental health issues.
fields.art_caption: Man on bench with his dogs

fields.title: Diabetes, obesity and HIV
fields.description: Diabetes and Obesity are common health issues worldwide and PLWH are more vulnerable to developing these conditions.  In this Ask the Expert session, participants will meet with diabetes and weight experts who will share information about the link between HIV and diabetes/obesity and discuss current treatment strategies and new technologies that can help people better control blood sugar and weight loss.  During the session, providers will be available to answer questions about diabetes prevention, diabetes management, and weight loss.

fields.title: Natural History of HIV and AIDS and opportunistic infections
fields.description:
What is the difference between HIV and AIDS? What do all the numbers mean when I get my blood drawn?  

For this month’s Ask the Expert session, our HIV specialists will provide participants with HIV 101, describing the natural course of HIV/AIDS, associated infections, the role of ART in changing the course of the infection, the impact of HIV on the aging body, and how to interpret all of those lab results.

fields.title: Bone Health and HIV
fields.description: Did you know that HIV and some HIV medications increase the risk of developing osteoporosis? During this month’s Ask the Expert session, we will be joined by doctors who specialize in bone health.  Our experts will answer questions on the basics of osteoporosis and related bone conditions, the relationship between HIV and bone health, how your doctors can evaluate osteoporosis, and how you can maintain healthy bones and avoid fractures.

fields.title: HIV medications - How to take them, potential interactions, Pre and Post Exposure Prophylaxis
fields.description:
What time of day should I take my ART? Should I take it with food? My doctor prescribed a new medication. Will it interact with my current ART?  

If you find yourself asking these sorts of questions, please join our experts during this Ask the Expert session. Our experts will review HIV medications, the best ways to take them, common medications that can interact with them, and more. Our experts will also review Prep and post-exposure prophylaxis, who should take them, and what testing they might need.

fields.title: Cardiovascular health in HIV
fields.description:
People with HIV are at significantly increased risk of developing cardiovascular disease, including heart attacks, strokes, and heart failure, and this risk increases as people age.  

In this month’s Ask the Expert session, one of our cardiologists will discuss the relationship between HIV and cardiovascular disease, other factors that can put patients at risk of cardiovascular illness, prevention strategies, and treatment regimens.  During this session, you will have the opportunity to ask this expert all of the important questions you have to help keep your heart as healthy as possible for as long as possible.

fields.title: Nutrition and HIV
fields.description:
Good nutrition is a cornerstone for healthy living.  Nutrition is especially important for people with HIV in order to help maintain a strong immune system.  

Join our nutrition experts in this Ask the Expert session to learn more about how food choices can help promote a strong immune system and keep you feeling as healthy as possible.  Our clinical dieticians will also help you make healthy choices within your budget, share meal/grocery list planning tools, and suggest community resources to further support a healthy diet.
fields.art_caption: Colorful array of fruits and vegetables

fields.title: Thriving, Resilient, and Empowered: Healthy Aging with HIV
fields.description: The event, held at Baruch College, will honor National HIV/AIDS Aging Awareness Day and be held on Wednesday, September 18, 2024 from 9:30am to 4:30pm. Attendees can look forward to engaging panel discussions focused on aging New Yorkers living with HIV; information and resource sharing by clinical and non-clinical service providers focused on aging populations; enlightening wellness activities; educational presentations; networking activities for service providers; and raffle giveaways. Light breakfast, lunch, and refreshments will be available for all attendees. All adults, adults with HIV, and clinical and non-clinical service providers that support aging New Yorkers are welcome!
fields.art_caption: National HIV/AIDS Aging Awareness Day Ribbon

fields.title: GMHC - Programs for Older Adults and Long-Term Survivors of HIV/AIDS
fields.description:
GMHC has developed an array of nationally recognized services to support the psychosocial and educational needs of adults aged 50 and older and LTS. Targeted services for adults ages 50 years and older and LTS include:

 - Healthy Aging Project
 - The Terry Brenneis and David Boger Hub for Long-Term Survivors
 - The Buddy Program
 - Thriving @ 50 and Beyond Group

fields.title: Free New York City Museums
fields.description:
These [New York City museums, memorials, and art-filled attractions](https://www.nyctourism.com/articles/free-museums-in-nyc/) are either always free, free on specific days of the week, or free for select hours. Find ones that interest you, and take advantage of their generosity.

It's important to note that this information is based on general admission only. Certain events and special exhibitions may still require a fee. Many spots have a pay-what-you-wish policy, though with a suggested admission price; in any case, donations are always encouraged. Also, keep in mind that some museums require advance reservations even for free admission, so it's best to check the website of your intended destination before your visit.
(From the NYC Tourism and Conventions Website)

fields.title: USDA MyPlate
fields.description:
[MyPlate](https://www.myplate.gov/life-stages/older-adults) is a website sponsored by the US Department of Agriculture. It offers tips and resources for healthy eating. 

Interested? Start with their [Older Adult Nutrition Quiz](https://www.fns.usda.gov/tn/quizzes/older-adult-nutrition)!
fields.art_caption: Good nutrition is essential to good health

fields.title: NYC Department for the Aging - Services
fields.description: [New York City Department for the Aging](https://www.nyc.gov/site/dfta/services/find-help.page) is the city's Area Agency on Aging. It sponsors many services, including older adult centers, nutrition support, and workforce programs. Most of these services are for people 60 or older.

fields.title: New York City Parks Events Calendar
fields.description:
The New York City Department of Parks and Recreation holds events in all five boroughs. You can use the events calendar to search by time of day, event type, and location. 


https://www.nycgovparks.org/events
fields.art_alt: People enjoying a New York City Park
fields.art_caption: People enjoying a New York City Park

fields.title: Caregiving Resources
fields.description:
We are often caregivers for friends and family. 

The National Institute on Aging offers many tips to help caregivers living with their loved one or caring at a distance. You can download a free handbook about caregiving [here](https://order.nia.nih.gov/sites/default/files/2023-03/caregivers-handbook-nia_0.pdf).
fields.art_caption: Caregiving is a fundamental part of life

fields.title: Elder Abuse
fields.description:
According to the New York State Office for the Aging (NYSOFA), "Elder abuse tragically impacts many adults aged 60 and older in New York State. It is estimated that 300,000 older New Yorkers are victimized annually." 
The
NYSOFA offers resources and links to help if you are a victim or suspect abuse of an older person in your life.
fields.art_alt: Picture of older person sitting alone looking out the window
fields.art_caption: There is help for victims of abuse

fields.title: Brooklyn Public Library
fields.description: The Brooklyn Public Library offers books and more - events, classes, and other services. Anyone who lives in New York State can get a library card.
fields.art_alt: Picture of shelves of books and long tables with chairs
fields.art_caption: Othmer Branch of the Brooklyn Public Library

fields.title: Aging Resources from HIV.gov
fields.description: Keep up with government blog posts related to HIV and Aging.

fields.title: National Resource Center on HIV and Aging
fields.description: This website, sponsored by GMHC, posts information about news, events, and resources for older people with HIV. It also offers information about health conditions.
fields.art_caption: Resources for Older Adults Living with HIV

fields.title: NATAP - National AIDS Treatment and Advocacy Project
fields.description:
This website is a curated repository of new stories, journal articles and webinars related to HIV and Aging. 

A Message from Jules Levin,
Executive Director, Editor, NATAP
 
As a person living with HIV and Hepatitis, I am well aware of the importance of having access to quality, current treatment information as well as having a group that will advocate and lobby on our behalf. I founded NATAP in order to address these needs.
fields.art_caption: National AIDS Treatment and Advocacy Project

fields.title: Myra Mahon Patient Resource Center
fields.description:
"The Myra Mahon Patient Resource Center aims to make accurate, science-based health information easily available so that patients and their families can make informed decisions about their care."

"Through its collection of online databases, pamphlets and staff, the center aims to live up to its namesake, Myra Mahon (1937-2011), a licensed clinical social worker who believed that 'an informed patient is almost always a healthier patient with a better chance for a favorable outcome.' Access to medical information helps patients overcome their fears, she said, while 'providing comfort and, many times, acceptance of treatment.'”
fields.art_alt: View of the Center includes a portrait of Myra Mahon
fields.art_caption: The Center's mission is to serve as a health information resource center for patients.

fields.title: MedlinePlus
fields.description:
"MedlinePlus is a service of the National Library of Medicine (NLM), the world's largest medical library, which is part of the National Institutes of Health (NIH)."

"Our mission is to present high-quality, relevant health and wellness information that is trusted, easy to understand, and free of advertising, in both English and Spanish—anywhere, anytime, on any device—for free."
fields.art_caption: MedlinePlus is an online health information resource of the National Library of Medicine

fields.title: New York Public Library
fields.description:
The New York Public Library (NYPL) offers books, exhibitions, classes, and much more.

If you are 13 or older and live, work, attend school, or pay property taxes in New York State, you can apply for a free library card [here](https://www.nypl.org/library-card/new)

Visit the [Polonsky Exhibit](https://www.nypl.org/spotlight/treasures) of the NYPL's treasures.
fields.art_alt: Librarian assisting a woman at the help desk
fields.art_caption: Need assistance? The Library is here to help.

fields.title: Community Gardens
fields.description:
GrowNYC has built more than 160 new gardens, including GreenThumb community gardens and our urban farm on Governors Island, as well as those in public housing developments, daycares, and senior centers. We build about ten new gardens a year and do renovation projects at an additional 25 spaces.

Interested in joining one of NYC's 600 existing community gardens? Find one at NYC Parks [GreenThumb](http://www.nycgovparks.org/greenthumb).
fields.art_alt: Garden featuring kale and cucumber plants
fields.art_caption: There are community gardens in all 5 boroughs.

fields.title: The Center at Red Oak
fields.description: This Harlem-based senior center has a wide variety of services, including health/wellness, housing, arts, workshops, meals, legal advice, social work assistance.

fields.title: The Alliance for Positive Change
fields.description: Alliance for Positive Change helps New Yorkers living with HIV and other chronic health conditions with healthcare, housing, harm reduction, coaching, and economic mobility through programs that equip people to navigate systemic inequities and achieve health and well-being.

fields.title: SAGE-NYC
fields.description:
SAGE offers "a second home" for LGBTQ+ elders in New York.

"Togetherness, friendship, community, and pride characterize SAGE’s five innovative senior centers in New York City. Each location—the Bronx, Brooklyn, Harlem, Midtown, and Staten Island—has a distinct style and offers a unique way to experience all SAGE has to offer."

fields.title: Center for Hearing and Healthy Aging
fields.description: "Whether you're an adult who was born with a hearing loss, has a newly diagnosed hearing loss or you're concerned about a loved one with hearing loss, you have found the right place.  At CHC, our mission is to provide high-quality, comprehensive services in partnership with highly skilled experts to empower people affected by hearing loss, deafness, or listening challenges."

fields.title: PAWS NY
fields.description:
For pet owners, their animals are an essential part of their families but also require a lot of care.

"Pets Are Wonderful Support (PAWS) NY provides services to vulnerable New Yorkers who need help caring for their pets due to physical and financial obstacles, with particular emphasis on low-income older adults and individuals living with illness or disability."

fields.title: NY Foundation for Senior Citizens
fields.description:
New York Foundation for Senior Citizens (NYFSC) is dedicated to helping New York’s older adults enjoy healthier, safer, more productive, and dignified lives in their homes and communities and to help them avoid the need for premature institutionalization. 

The organization can help link older adults in NYC to various resources, including older adult centers, home repair services, transportation, and emergency support.  In addition, they offer additional ways to engage with the community, including discounted theater tickets.
fields.art_alt: Older women sitting at dinning table

fields.title: God's Love We Deliver
fields.description:
A meal delivery service that is free to its clients regardless of income.  

The mission of God's Love We Deliver is to "improve the health and well-being of people living with HIV/AIDS, cancer, and other serious illnesses by alleviating hunger and malnutrition."

It is a non-sectarian organization.
fields.art_alt: God's Love We Deliver Team photo
fields.art_caption: God's Love We Deliver Team in Kitchen

fields.title: MTA Reduced Fares for Older Adults
fields.description: The MTA offers a reduced fare MetroCard for riders who are 65 or older or riders who have qualifying disabilities. With the reduced fare card, fares for the subway, buses, and express buses are cut in half.  Cardholders are also eligible for reduced fares on some of the LIRR and MetroNorth services. For more information or to submit an application for a reduced fare MetroCard, please visit the MTA website at [MTA] (https://new.mta.info/fares/reduced-fare).

fields.title: CaringKind
fields.description: CaringKind is an organization that creates, delivers, and promotes comprehensive and compassionate care and support services for individuals and families affected by Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias. The organization also works to eliminate Alzheimer’s disease through the advancement of research. They provide programs and services for individuals with dementia, their family, and professional caregivers; increase public awareness; collaborate with research centers; and inform public policy through advocacy. For more information, please visit their website [here] (https://www.caringkindnyc.org/).

fields.title: James Baldwin: Mountain to Fire
fields.description:
As part of a program of events and exhibits celebrating the 100th anniversary of James Baldwin's birth, the Polonsky Exhibition of The New York Public Library's Treasures invites you to come discover early manuscripts and other items related to Baldwin's work. The exhibit is now on display at the Stephen A. Schwarzman Building.

Stephen A. Schwarzman Building.
Fifth Avenue and 42nd Street

fields.title: JIMMY! God’s Black Revolutionary Mouth
fields.description:
"Novelist, essayist, intellectual, and activist James Baldwin (1924 - 1987) is renowned as one of the world’s most influential and prophetic voices of our time. His death in 1987 sent waves of grief around the world. Amiri Baraka’s eulogy, titled “Jimmy!”, spoke of James "Jimmy" Baldwin as “not only a writer, international literary figure” but as a “man, spirit, voice”. Baraka called Baldwin “God’s black revolutionary mouth” which speaks to Baldwin’s enduring legacy of radical truth-telling. 

The Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture is home to Baldwin’s archive of personal papers. In celebration of his 100th birthday, on public display for the first time, we proudly present selections from the James Baldwin Papers that highlight his literary career and legacy from childhood to death, along with items from other research collections that illuminate the passion, brilliance, and courageous spirit of James “Jimmy” Baldwin.

Organized by Barrye Brown, Curator, Manuscripts, Archives, and Rare Books Division at the Schomburg Center."

Open from August 2, 2024 - February 28, 2025

The Schomberg Center for Research in Black Culture 
515 Malcolm X Boulevard (135th St and Malcolm X Blvd)
New York, NY 10037
